positions.title: Senior Software Architect
positions.description: After a short break from being an adult (went back to school full time to finish my Mathematics degree), I landed a gig at Network Instruments developing network packet analysis software. I was mostly charged with adding parallelism and updating the code to be 64-bit compatible. Which I did, and it worked great. Then I found some bugs in the co-owner's goto-riddled code, and then I stood my ground when the development plan included creating a heinous, unmaintainable nightmare. Then I got fired. Thank goodness.

positions.title: Windows Application Developer
positions.description:
Developing device drivers always seemed like something so difficult to do that they remained the domain of the true badass developers. In 2006, I got a chance to try my hand at them. I developed Windows (and a pinch of Linux) device drivers for Focus Enhancements' video output boards. They worked well, which basically means you never noticed them, and I was officially done with that. If device drivers are only written by the badass developers, I don't want to be a badass.

In full disclosure, I've since done other device drivers, and I don't find them as annoying as I once did, but they will always be mind numbingly boring.

positions.title: Lead Software Developer
positions.description:
Early in 2004, my soon-to-be father-in-law's company, Portage Interactive, needed someone to help the company take on an opportunity. Paxton/Patterson needed someone to update and maintain the software behind it's learning management systems. For a couple of years, I was basically the guy that did that. I built out the server, client, and mobile (Palm) and had fancy installers that pushed all that out in fancy, easy-to-use, ways.

http://www.paxtonpatterson.com

positions.title: Lead Software Developer
positions.description:
With only a few months of programming under my belt, I managed to convince a wonderful owner of a kiosk manufacturing company to let me program kiosk management software for him. Realistically, I barely knew how to program when I was hired. Nonetheless, within a month I was writing credit card drivers and a year later my software was on kiosks at the 2000 Democratic National Convention.

http://partners.nytimes.com/library/politics/camp/081400wh-dem-wired.html

positions.title: Student Engineer, Thermofoil Heater Department
positions.description: Taught myself to program in Visual Basic for Applications while doing a student internship for the Aerospace Engineering program I was in at the University of Minnesota. Also discovered that I did not want to be an Aerospace Engineer.
